notes:
1. Meaning of State Executive

  • The State Executive is the executive branch of Government at the State level.

It is responsible for:

  • Administration of the State.
  • Implementation of laws.
  • Maintenance of law and order.
  • Execution of Government policies.
  • Delivery of public services.
  • Administration of State departments.
  • Like the Union Executive, it operates under the Parliamentary system of government.
📌 Must-Memorise

State Executive → Parliamentary System at State Level

2. Constitutional Framework

The core State Executive provisions are contained in:

  • Part VI — The States.
  • Articles 153–167.

These provisions deal principally with:

  • Governor.
  • Chief Minister.
  • Council of Ministers.
  • Advocate General.
📌 Must-Memorise

State Executive → Part VI → Articles 153–167

3. Composition of State Executive

The State Executive consists of:

  • Governor.
  • Chief Minister.
  • Council of Ministers.
  • Advocate General.
  • There is no constitutional office corresponding to the Union Vice-President at the State level.

4. Constitutional Head and Real Executive

Governor:

  • Constitutional Head.
  • Nominal Executive.
  • Executive power formally vested in the office.

Chief Minister:

  • Real Executive.
  • Head of State Government.
  • Head of Council of Ministers.

Council of Ministers:

  • Exercises actual executive authority.
  • Aids and advises Governor.
📌 Must-Memorise

Governor → Constitutional Head

Chief Minister → Real Executive

5. Article 154

  • Article 154 vests executive power of the State in the Governor.

In practice, this power is generally exercised through:

  • Chief Minister.
  • Council of Ministers.
  • This reflects the Parliamentary form of Government.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 154 → Executive Power of State → Governor

6. Parliamentary System at State Level

The State-level parliamentary structure means:

  • Governor is Constitutional Head.
  • Chief Minister is Real Executive.
  • Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to Legislative Assembly.
  • Government remains in office only while enjoying Assembly confidence.

7. Dual Executive

Nominal Executive:

  • Governor.

Real Executive:

  • Chief Minister.
  • Council of Ministers.
  • This broadly corresponds to the President–Prime Minister relationship at Union level.

8. Collective Responsibility

  • Article 164(2) provides collective responsibility of Council of Ministers to Legislative Assembly.

If Assembly passes a No-Confidence Motion:

  • Entire Ministry must resign.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 164(2) → Collective Responsibility → Legislative Assembly

9. Executive Accountability

The State Executive is accountable through:

  • Question Hour.
  • Zero Hour.
  • Calling Attention.
  • Adjournment Motions.
  • Censure Motion.
  • No-Confidence Motion.
  • Budget discussions.
  • Legislative Committees.

10. Constitutional Supremacy

The State Executive derives authority from:

  • Constitution of India.

Its actions remain subject to:

  • Judicial Review.
  • Rule of Law.
  • Constitutional limitations.
  • Neither Governor nor elected Government may act contrary to the Constitution.

11. Article 153 — Governor

  • Article 153 provides for a Governor for each State.

The same person may be appointed Governor of:

  • Two or more States.
  • The attachment associates this arrangement with the Seventh Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 153 → Governor

Same Person → Governor of Two or More States

12. Governor's Constitutional Position

The Governor is:

  • Constitutional Head.
  • Nominal Executive.
  • Constitutional link between Union and State.
  • Authority performing specified constitutional functions.
  • Expected ordinarily to act on ministerial advice.

13. Article 155 — Appointment of Governor

Governor is appointed by:

  • President of India.
  • Appointment is made by warrant under the President's hand and seal.

Governor is:

  • Not directly elected.
  • Not indirectly elected.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 155 → Governor Appointed by President

14. Why Governor Is Appointed

The Constituent Assembly preferred appointment rather than election to avoid:

  • Rival political authority between Governor and Chief Minister.
  • Conflict within parliamentary government.
  • Creation of two competing democratic mandates.

The system also sought:

  • Constitutional neutrality.
  • National unity.
  • Continuity.

15. Article 157 — Qualifications

A Governor must:

  • Be a citizen of India.
  • Have completed 35 years of age.
📌 Must-Memorise

Governor → Indian Citizen + 35 Years

16. Article 158 — Conditions of Office

Governor:

  • Cannot remain a Member of Parliament.
  • Cannot remain a Member of State Legislature.
  • Cannot hold another office of profit.
  • Is entitled to official residence.
  • Receives salary and allowances determined by Parliament.

17. Legislative Seat on Becoming Governor

If an MP or State legislator becomes Governor:

  • Legislative seat becomes vacant upon entering the Governor's office.

18. Governor's Emoluments

Governor receives:

  • Salary.
  • Allowances.
  • Official residence.
  • Other privileges prescribed by law.
  • Expenditure relating to Governor is charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State according to the attachment.

19. Article 159 — Governor's Oath

Oath is administered by:

  • Chief Justice of the High Court.

In the Chief Justice's absence:

  • Senior-most available Judge of the High Court.
📌 Must-Memorise

Governor's Oath → Chief Justice of High Court

20. Contents of Governor's Oath

Governor undertakes to:

  • Faithfully perform duties.
  • Preserve, protect and defend Constitution.
  • Serve and promote well-being of people of the State.

21. Article 156 — Term

Normal term:

  • Five years.

Governor nevertheless holds office:

  • During pleasure of President.
  • Five-year tenure is therefore not an absolute guaranteed tenure.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 156 → 5 Years + Pleasure of President

22. Continuance after Five Years

Governor may continue after expiry of five-year term:

  • Until successor assumes office.

23. Governor's Resignation

Governor resigns by writing to:

  • President of India.
📌 Must-Memorise

Governor Resignation → President

24. Removal of Governor

  • Governor is not removed through impeachment.
  • Governor may be removed by President under pleasure doctrine.
  • The attachment emphasises that Governor does not enjoy the President's impeachment protection.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

President → Impeachment

Governor → No Impeachment

25. Vacancy in Governor's Office

Vacancy may arise due to:

  • Expiry of term.
  • Resignation.
  • Removal.
  • Death.
  • Transfer.
  • Other constitutional cause.
  • Article 160 provides arrangements for contingencies.

26. Article 160

  • Article 160 allows arrangements for discharge of Governor's functions in contingencies not otherwise provided for.

27. Governor's Immunities

The attachment identifies constitutional protections including:

  • No criminal proceedings during tenure.
  • No arrest or imprisonment during tenure.
  • Specified notice for personal civil proceedings.
  • Protection regarding exercise of official constitutional functions.
📌 Must-Memorise

Governor Immunity → Article 361

28. Article 361

Article 361 contains important constitutional immunities relating to:

  • President.
  • Governors.
  • These protections preserve independence and dignity of constitutional office.

29. Governor's Powers — Overview

Major categories include:

  • Executive powers.
  • Legislative powers.
  • Financial powers.
  • Judicial powers.
  • Discretionary powers.
  • Emergency-related functions.

30. Appointment of Chief Minister

  • Governor appoints Chief Minister under Article 164.

Normally:

  • Leader commanding majority in Legislative Assembly is appointed.

In a hung Assembly:

  • Governor invites person most likely to command confidence.
  • Majority must subsequently be proved on floor of House.

31. Appointment of Ministers

Governor appoints other Ministers:

  • On advice of Chief Minister.

Chief Minister effectively determines:

  • Ministerial selection.
  • Portfolio allocation.
  • Reshuffle.
  • Removal recommendations.

32. Appointment of Advocate General

Under Article 165:

  • Governor appoints Advocate General.
  • Advocate General is highest law officer of State.

33. State Election Commissioner

Under Article 243K:

  • Governor appoints State Election Commissioner.

State Election Commission supervises elections connected with:

  • Panchayats.
  • Municipalities.

34. State Public Service Commission

Under Article 316:

  • Governor appoints Chairperson and Members of State Public Service Commission.

35. Article 166 — State Government Business

  • All State executive action is expressed to be taken in Governor's name.

Rules regulate:

  • Transaction of Government business.
  • Allocation of work among Ministers.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 166 → Conduct of State Government Business

36. Governor and State Legislature

  • Governor is an integral part of State Legislature.
  • Governor is not necessarily a member of either House.
  • Detailed legislative structure belongs to Chapter 14.

37. Article 174

Governor may:

  • Summon State Legislature.
  • Prorogue State Legislature.
  • Dissolve Legislative Assembly.
  • These powers are ordinarily exercised on ministerial advice, subject to limited constitutional situations.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 174 → Summon + Prorogue + Dissolve Assembly

38. Article 175

Governor may:

  • Address either House.
  • Send messages to State Legislature.

39. Article 176

Governor addresses:

  • First session after each General Election.
  • First session of every year.

Address generally outlines:

  • Government policies.
  • Legislative programme.
  • Administrative priorities.

40. Article 200 — Assent to State Bills

Governor may:

  • Give assent.
  • Withhold assent.
  • Return a Bill other than a Money Bill.
  • Reserve a Bill for President.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 200 → Governor's Assent to State Bills

41. Return of State Bill

  • Governor may return an eligible Bill for reconsideration.
  • Money Bill cannot be returned in this manner according to the framework in the attachment.

42. Article 201

When Governor reserves a Bill:

  • President considers it under Article 201.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 200 → Governor Reservation

Article 201 → President Considers Reserved Bill

43. Article 213 — Ordinance

  • Governor may promulgate Ordinance when State Legislature is not in session.
  • Ordinance has legislative force temporarily.
  • It must receive legislative approval within six weeks of reassembly.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 213 → Governor's Ordinance

44. Nature of Ordinance Power

Ordinance power is generally exercised:

  • On advice of Council of Ministers.
  • It is not ordinarily an independent discretionary power.

45. State Budget

  • Annual Financial Statement or State Budget is laid before State Legislature in Governor's name.
  • Governor therefore performs an important constitutional role in State financial procedure.

46. Money Bills at State Level

A Money Bill can be introduced in State Legislature:

  • Only with prior recommendation of Governor.
📌 Must-Memorise

State Money Bill → Governor's Prior Recommendation

47. Demands for Grants

  • Demands for Grants are presented with Governor's recommendation.

48. Contingency Fund of State

Governor administers Contingency Fund of State according to:

  • Constitutional provisions.
  • State law.

49. Article 161 — Pardoning Power

Governor may grant:

  • Pardon.
  • Reprieve.
  • Respite.
  • Remission.
  • Suspension.
  • Commutation

for offences against laws relating to matters within State executive power.

📌 Must-Memorise

Article 161 → Governor's Clemency Power

50. Governor and Court-Martial

  • The attachment states that Governor does not possess pardoning power over Court-Martial sentences.
  • This distinguishes Article 161 from President's Article 72 power.

51. Governor and Death Sentence

The attached notes distinguish President and Governor as follows:

President:

  • May pardon death sentence.

Governor:

  • Cannot grant pardon of death sentence under the framework stated in the source.
  • May exercise suspension, remission or commutation where constitutionally applicable.

52. President vs Governor — Executive Powers

President:

  • Article 53.
  • Union executive power.

Governor:

  • Article 154.
  • State executive power.

53. President vs Governor — Clemency

President:

  • Article 72.

Governor:

  • Article 161.

54. President vs Governor — Ordinance

President:

  • Article 123.

Governor:

  • Article 213.

55. President vs Governor — Government Formation

President:

  • Appoints Prime Minister.

Governor:

  • Appoints Chief Minister.

56. Article 163

  • There shall be Council of Ministers with Chief Minister at head to aid and advise Governor.
  • Governor ordinarily acts on this advice.
  • Limited discretion may exist where Constitution permits it.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 163 → Aid and Advice + Limited Governor Discretion

57. General Rule on Governor's Discretion

  • Ministerial advice is the general rule.

Discretion is:

  • Limited.
  • Exceptional.
  • Situation-specific.
  • Constitutionally controlled.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Governor's Discretion → Exception, Not Rule

58. Appointment in Hung Assembly

Governor may exercise limited discretion when:

  • No party has majority.
  • Coalition claims compete.
  • No obvious Chief Ministerial candidate exists.
  • Person invited must prove majority through Floor Test.

59. Floor Test

When majority is genuinely doubtful:

  • Floor Test is proper constitutional method.
  • Legislative Assembly determines majority.
  • Governor's subjective opinion is not a substitute for House confidence.
📌 Must-Memorise

Majority Doubt → Floor Test

60. Dismissal of Ministry

  • Governor cannot dismiss Ministry merely because of personal disagreement.

If Government appears to lose majority:

  • Floor Test should establish actual position.
  • If Ministry loses confidence and refuses to resign, constitutional consequences may follow.

61. Dissolution of Assembly

Normally Governor dissolves Assembly:

  • On Chief Minister/Council advice.

Exceptional discretion may arise where:

  • No stable Government appears possible.
  • Such discretion remains constitutionally reviewable.

62. Reservation of Bills

  • Governor may reserve specified Bills for President under Article 200.

Situations identified in the source include Bills:

  • Constitutionally requiring reservation.
  • Potentially affecting High Court powers.
  • Requiring Presidential consideration.

After reservation:

  • President acts under Article 201.

63. Article 356 Report

  • Governor may report to President where State Government cannot be carried on according to Constitution.
  • Detailed treatment belongs to Centre–State Relations.
  • Governor's report is not beyond judicial review.

64. Constitutional and Situational Discretion

Constitutional discretion:

  • Express constitutional basis.

Example:

  • Reserving Bill for President.

Situational discretion:

  • Arises from political circumstances and constitutional conventions.

Example:

  • Appointment of Chief Minister in hung Assembly.

65. Limits on Governor's Discretion

Discretion is subject to:

  • Constitution.
  • Judicial Review.
  • Constitutional conventions.
  • Democratic principles.
  • Constitutional morality.

Governor cannot:

  • Act arbitrarily.
  • Become alternative Government.
  • Interfere routinely in day-to-day administration.

66. Sarkaria Commission

The Sarkaria Commission, 1983–1988, recommended:

  • Political neutrality of Governor.
  • Floor Test for determining majority.
  • Article 356 only as last resort.
  • Avoidance of unnecessary interference.
  • Constitutional impartiality.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sarkaria Commission → Governor Neutrality + Floor Test + Article 356 Last Resort

67. Punchhi Commission

The Punchhi Commission, 2007–2010, recommended:

  • Clearer guidelines on Governor's discretionary power.
  • Greater transparency in appointment.
  • Fixed tenure except exceptional circumstances.
  • Restrained Article 356 use.
  • Stronger cooperative federalism.

68. Chief Minister — Constitutional Position

  • Chief Minister is Real Executive at State level.
  • Position broadly parallels Prime Minister at Union level.
  • Governor is Constitutional Head.
  • Chief Minister heads actual elected Government.
📌 Must-Memorise

Chief Minister → Real Executive + Head of State Government

69. Chief Minister — Important Articles

Principal Articles:

  • Article 163.
  • Article 164.
  • Article 166.
  • Article 167.

70. Appointment of Chief Minister

  • Governor appoints Chief Minister under Article 164.

Normally:

  • Majority-party or majority-coalition leader.

Hung Assembly:

  • Governor may invite leader most likely to command confidence.

71. Qualifications of Chief Minister

  • Constitution does not prescribe separate special qualifications exclusively for Chief Minister.
  • Chief Minister must be qualified to become a member of State Legislature.

72. Chief Minister and Legislative Membership

Chief Minister may ordinarily be:

  • Member of Legislative Assembly.
  • Member of Legislative Council where one exists.

73. Six-Month Rule for Chief Minister

  • Non-legislator may be appointed Chief Minister.

Must become member of State Legislature within:

  • Six months.
  • Otherwise must cease to hold office.
📌 Must-Memorise

Non-Legislator CM → 6 Months

74. Chief Minister's Oath

Chief Minister takes:

  • Oath of Office.
  • Oath of Secrecy.

Administered by:

  • Governor.

75. Chief Minister's Tenure

  • Constitution prescribes no fixed tenure.

Chief Minister remains in office as long as:

  • Legislative Assembly confidence is retained.

76. End of Chief Minister's Office

Chief Minister may leave office due to:

  • Resignation.
  • Loss of majority.
  • Death.
  • Successful No-Confidence Motion.

When Chief Minister resigns:

  • Entire Council of Ministers ordinarily goes with the Chief Minister.

77. Chief Minister and Ministers

Chief Minister:

  • Selects Ministers.
  • Recommends appointments.
  • Allocates portfolios.
  • Reshuffles departments.
  • Advises removal of Ministers.

78. Chief Minister as Policy Leader

Chief Minister:

  • Frames Government policy.
  • Coordinates administration.
  • Supervises welfare programmes.
  • Directs State departments.
  • Acts as principal State-level political policy-maker.

79. Chief Minister in Legislature

Where Chief Minister is an Assembly member, the office generally:

  • Leads Government in House.
  • Defends policies.
  • Answers major debates.
  • Guides legislative business.

80. Link between Governor and Council

Chief Minister is principal communication channel between:

  • Governor.
  • Council of Ministers.
  • This relationship is constitutionally reinforced by Article 167.

81. Article 167 — Communicating Decisions

Chief Minister must communicate to Governor:

  • Decisions of Council of Ministers.
  • Administrative matters.
  • Legislative proposals.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 167 → CM's Duties towards Governor

82. Article 167 — Furnishing Information

Governor may require information concerning:

  • State administration.
  • Legislative affairs.
  • Chief Minister must furnish such information.

83. Article 167 — Individual Minister's Decision

If Governor requires:

Chief Minister must place before Council of Ministers any matter:

  • Decided by an individual Minister.
  • Not yet considered collectively.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

Article 167 → Supports Collective Decision-Making

84. Chief Minister in Federal Forums

Chief Minister may:

  • Represent State in Inter-State Council meetings.
  • Attend meetings convened by Union Government.
  • Coordinate national programmes.
  • Represent State interests in federal forums.

85. Council of Ministers

  • Council of Ministers is real collective executive authority.
  • Headed by Chief Minister.
  • Aids and advises Governor.
  • Formulates policies.
  • Administers departments.
  • Implements laws.

86. Appointment of State Ministers

Governor appoints Ministers:

  • On advice of Chief Minister.
  • Chief Minister effectively controls composition of Ministry.

87. Oath of Ministers

Every Minister takes:

  • Oath of Office.
  • Oath of Secrecy.

Administered by:

  • Governor.

88. Categories of Ministers

By constitutional practice, Council may include:

  • Cabinet Ministers.
  • Ministers of State.
  • Deputy Ministers.
  • Constitution itself does not formally classify these categories.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Minister Categories → Practice

Not Express Constitutional Classification

89. Cabinet Ministers

Cabinet Ministers:

  • Senior-most Ministers.
  • Head major departments.
  • Formulate important Government policies.
  • Participate in Cabinet meetings.
  • Take major executive decisions.

90. Ministers of State

May:

  • Assist Cabinet Ministers.
  • Hold independent charge of smaller departments.
  • Assist in larger Ministries.

91. Deputy Ministers

  • Assist Cabinet Ministers and Ministers of State.
  • Do not ordinarily attend Cabinet unless invited.

92. Cabinet

  • Cabinet is inner core of Council of Ministers.
  • Consists of senior Ministers.

Principal decision-making body on:

  • Policy.
  • Administration.
  • Legislation.
  • Finance.
  • Law and order.
  • Cabinet decisions bind all Ministers.

93. Cabinet vs Council of Ministers

Cabinet:

  • Smaller.
  • Senior Ministers.
  • Major policy decisions.
  • Inner decision-making core.

Council of Ministers:

  • Larger.
  • Includes all ministerial categories.
  • Real collective executive.
  • Collectively responsible to Assembly.

94. Collective Responsibility of Ministers

Under Article 164(2):

  • Entire Ministry acts as one political unit.
  • All Ministers stand or fall together.
  • Loss of Assembly confidence requires resignation of entire Council.

95. Individual Responsibility

  • Each Minister is responsible for department assigned.
  • Appointment and removal formally involve Governor.

In practice:

  • Chief Minister's advice is central.

96. Six-Month Rule for Ministers

  • Non-legislator may become Minister.

Must become member of State Legislature within:

  • Six months.
  • Otherwise ceases to hold office.

97. Size of State Council of Ministers

The attachment states that under 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003:

Total Ministers including Chief Minister cannot exceed:

  • 15% of total Legislative Assembly strength.

State Ministry must ordinarily have:

  • At least 12 Ministers.
📌 Must-Memorise

91st Amendment → State Ministry ≤ 15% of Assembly

Minimum → 12 Ministers

98. Policy Functions of Council

Council of Ministers:

  • Frames State policies.
  • Determines administrative priorities.
  • Approves welfare programmes.
  • Formulates development strategies.

99. Administrative Functions

Council:

  • Supervises departments.
  • Implements laws.
  • Executes schemes.
  • Coordinates departments.

100. Legislative Functions

Council:

  • Introduces Government Bills.
  • Advises Governor on summoning Legislature.
  • Conducts Government legislative business.
  • Defends policies in Legislature.

101. Financial Functions

Council:

  • Prepares State Budget.
  • Approves expenditure proposals.
  • Recommends introduction of financial measures.
  • Supervises State financial administration.

102. Cabinet Meetings

  • Convened by Chief Minister.
  • Presided over by Chief Minister.

Major subjects include:

  • Policy.
  • Bills.
  • Administrative reform.
  • Budget.
  • Law and order.
  • Development programmes.

103. Effect of Chief Minister's Resignation

  • Council of Ministers exists under Chief Minister's leadership.

When Chief Minister resigns:

  • Entire Council ceases as a Ministry.

104. Article 165 — Advocate General

Advocate General is:

  • Highest law officer of State.
  • Principal legal adviser to State Government.

Constitutional basis:

  • Article 165.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 165 → Advocate General

105. Appointment of Advocate General

Appointed by:

  • Governor.
  • Appointment is ordinarily made within constitutional Government framework.

106. Advocate General Qualifications

A person must be qualified to become:

  • Judge of a High Court.

The attachment identifies requirements such as:

  • Citizen of India.
  • Judicial office for at least 10 years, or
  • Advocate of High Court(s) for at least 10 years.

107. Advocate General's Tenure

  • No fixed constitutional tenure.

Holds office during:

  • Pleasure of Governor.

108. Advocate General's Remuneration

  • Remuneration is determined by Governor.
  • Constitution does not prescribe fixed salary.

109. Advocate General's Functions

Advocate General:

  • Advises State Government.
  • Advises on constitutional issues.
  • Advises on legislation.
  • Advises on administrative legal disputes.
  • Represents State in courts.
  • Performs legal duties assigned by Governor.

110. Advocate General in Courts

Advocate General may represent State before:

  • High Court.
  • Supreme Court.
  • Other courts.
  • Tribunals

when required.

111. Advocate General in Legislature

Advocate General may:

  • Speak in State Legislature.
  • Participate in discussions.
  • Participate in committees where permitted.

But:

  • Cannot vote merely by virtue of office.
📌 Must-Memorise

Advocate General → Can Speak, Cannot Vote

112. Advocate General vs Attorney General

Advocate General:

  • State.
  • Article 165.
  • Appointed by Governor.
  • Advises State Government.

Attorney General:

  • Union.
  • Article 76.
  • Appointed by President.
  • Advises Union Government.

113. Governor–Chief Minister Relationship

Core principle:

  • Governor → Constitutional Head.
  • Chief Minister → Real Executive.
  • Governor ordinarily acts on aid and advice.
  • Chief Minister serves as principal adviser and communication channel.

114. Governor Is Not an Alternative Executive

  • Article 163 does not create a parallel elected Government.
  • Governor ordinarily follows ministerial advice.
  • Discretion operates only within limited constitutional areas.

115. Appointment and Removal of Ministers

  • Governor formally appoints Ministers.
  • Chief Minister determines composition through advice.
  • Removal of a Minister is ordinarily based on Chief Minister's advice.

116. Allocation of Portfolios

Chief Minister determines:

  • Department distribution.
  • Portfolio allocation.
  • Reshuffles.
  • Governor formally gives effect according to State business procedure.

117. Legislature and Governor–CM Relationship

Governor summons Legislature ordinarily on:

  • Council of Ministers' advice.

Governor's Bill-related powers must operate within:

  • Constitution.
  • Judicial precedents.
  • Parliamentary conventions.

118. Collective Responsibility Is to Assembly

Council of Ministers is collectively responsible:

  • To Legislative Assembly.
  • It is not politically responsible to Governor.
  • Governor cannot remove elected Government merely because of personal disagreement.
📌 Must-Memorise

State Ministry → Responsible to Legislative Assembly, Not Governor

119. Constitutional Conventions

Healthy Governor–Chief Minister relations require:

  • Mutual respect.
  • Constitutional morality.
  • Political neutrality.
  • Cooperation.
  • Respect for democratic mandate.

120. Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab, 1974

Supreme Court held:

  • Governor is Constitutional Head.
  • Governor ordinarily acts on aid and advice of Council of Ministers.
  • Independent discretion is limited to constitutionally recognised areas.
📌 Must-Memorise

Shamsher Singh → 1974 → Governor Acts on Ministerial Advice

121. S.R. Bommai v. Union of India, 1994

Supreme Court held:

  • Majority should ordinarily be tested on floor of Assembly.
  • Governor's Article 356 report is subject to judicial review.
  • President's Rule cannot be used arbitrarily.
📌 Must-Memorise

S.R. Bommai → 1994 → Floor Test + Article 356 Judicial Review

122. Jagdambika Pal Case, 1998

  • Supreme Court directed an immediate Floor Test amid political uncertainty in Uttar Pradesh.
  • It reinforced House-based determination of majority.

123. Har Sharan Verma v. Tribhuvan Narain Singh, 1971

  • A non-legislator may be appointed Chief Minister.
  • Person must become legislator within six months.
📌 Must-Memorise

Har Sharan Verma → Non-Legislator CM + 6-Month Rule

124. S.R. Chaudhuri v. State of Punjab, 2001

  • Non-legislator Minister may serve only within six-month constitutional window.
  • Repeated reappointment without election was held impermissible.
📌 Must-Memorise

S.R. Chaudhuri → 2001 → No Repeated Six-Month Reappointment

125. Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India, 2006

Supreme Court held:

  • Premature dissolution without allowing democratic process or Floor Test may be unconstitutional.
  • Political speculation cannot substitute constitutional proof.
  • Governor's discretion is reviewable and limited.

126. B.P. Singhal v. Union of India, 2010

Supreme Court held:

  • Governor holds office during President's pleasure.

Removal cannot be:

  • Arbitrary.
  • Capricious.
  • Purely political.
  • Constitutional basis must exist even if reasons are not publicly disclosed.
📌 Must-Memorise

B.P. Singhal → 2010 → Governor Removal Not Arbitrary

127. Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker, 2016

Supreme Court held:

  • Governor cannot unnecessarily interfere with legislative proceedings.
  • Discretion must remain within constitutional limits.
  • Governor cannot direct proceedings without constitutional authority.
📌 Must-Memorise

Nabam Rebia → 2016 → Limits on Governor's Legislative Intervention

128. Shivraj Singh Chouhan v. Speaker, 2020

Supreme Court held:

When majority is doubtful:

  • Floor Test is proper constitutional method.
  • Democratic legitimacy is determined inside Legislature.

129. Keisham Meghachandra Singh, 2020

Supreme Court stated defection petitions should ordinarily be decided within:

  • Three months.
  • The principle is relevant to stability of State Governments.

Ministers and Advocate General may:

134. Seventh Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956

The attachment associates the amendment with:

  • State reorganisation.
  • Amendment of Article 153.
  • Permitting same individual to serve as Governor of two or more States.

7th Amendment → One Governor for Two or More States

135. Forty-Second Amendment Act, 1976

The attachment connects the 42nd Amendment with:

  • Emergency-period strengthening of governmental authority.
  • Expansion of Directive Principles.

Addition of:

  • Socialist.
  • Secular.
  • Integrity

to Preamble.

  • Several Emergency-era changes were later modified.

136. Forty-Fourth Amendment Act, 1978

The attachment emphasises:

  • Restoration of democratic safeguards.
  • Checks and balances.
  • Restrictions on misuse of Emergency provisions.
  • Reinforcement of responsible government.

137. Fifty-Second Amendment Act, 1985

  • Introduced Anti-Defection Law.
  • Inserted Tenth Schedule.
  • Strengthened political stability and party discipline.

138. Seventy-Third Amendment Act, 1992

  • Gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj.
  • Article 243K provides for State Election Commissioner appointed by Governor.
  • Strengthened democratic decentralisation.

139. Seventy-Fourth Amendment Act, 1992

  • Gave constitutional status to Municipalities.
  • Expanded State's constitutional role in urban local governance.

140. Ninety-First Amendment Act, 2003

State Executive effects include:

  • Ministry limited to 15% of Assembly strength.
  • Minimum of 12 Ministers under framework stated in attachment.
  • One-third split protection removed.
  • Two-thirds merger retained.
  • Defectors restricted from becoming Ministers until constitutionally eligible.

141. One Hundred and First Amendment Act, 2016

  • Introduced GST.
  • Required greater Union–State coordination.
  • State Finance Ministers participate in GST Council framework.
  • Strengthened cooperative federalism.

142. One Hundred and Third Amendment Act, 2019

  • Introduced EWS reservation.
  • Implementation at State level involves State executive machinery according to constitutional and legal framework.

143. Governor vs Chief Minister

Governor:

  • Constitutional Head.
  • Appointed by President.
  • Nominal Executive.
  • Generally acts on advice.
  • Symbolises constitutional continuity.

Chief Minister:

  • Real Executive.
  • Appointed by Governor.
  • Heads elected Government.
  • Advises Governor.
  • Exercises practical executive leadership.

144. President vs Governor

President:

  • Union.
  • Elected indirectly.
  • Article 53.
  • Article 72 clemency.
  • Article 123 Ordinance.
  • Removal through impeachment.

Governor:

  • State.
  • Appointed by President.
  • Article 154.
  • Article 161 clemency.
  • Article 213 Ordinance.
  • Holds office during President's pleasure.

145. Attorney General vs Advocate General

Attorney General:

  • Union.
  • Article 76.
  • Appointed by President.

Advocate General:

  • State.
  • Article 165.
  • Appointed by Governor.

Both:

  • Highest law officers at respective levels.
  • May participate in legislative proceedings.
  • Cannot vote merely by virtue of office.

Which Part contains State Executive provisions? → Part VI.

What are the core State Executive Articles? → Articles 153–167.

Which Article provides for Governor? → Article 153.

Can the same person be Governor of two or more States? → Yes.

Who appoints Governor? → President.

Which Article provides for appointment? → Article 155.

Is Governor directly or indirectly elected? → Neither; appointed by President.

Which Article provides qualifications? → Article 157.

What are the constitutional qualifications? → Indian citizen and completed 35 years.

Which Article deals with Governor's conditions of office? → Article 158.

Can Governor remain an MP or MLA? → No.

Can Governor hold an office of profit? → No.

Who administers Governor's oath? → Chief Justice of High Court or senior-most available Judge.

Which Article deals with oath? → Article 159.

What is normal Governor's term? → Five years.

Does Governor have guaranteed five-year tenure? → No.

During whose pleasure does Governor hold office? → President.

Which Article deals with term? → Article 156.

To whom does Governor resign? → President.

Can Governor be impeached? → No.

Which Article deals with contingencies concerning Governor's functions? → Article 160.

Which Article gives Governor pardoning power? → Article 161.

Can Governor deal with Court-Martial punishment under the framework in the attached notes? → No.

Which Article defines extent of State executive power? → Article 162.

Which Article provides Council of Ministers to aid and advise Governor? → Article 163.

Is Governor's discretion the general rule? → No; it is exceptional.

Who appoints Chief Minister? → Governor.

Which Article principally governs appointment of CM and Ministers? → Article 164.

To which House is State Council of Ministers collectively responsible? → Legislative Assembly.

Which clause provides collective responsibility? → Article 164(2).

Can a non-legislator become Chief Minister? → Yes.

Within how long must the person become a State legislator? → Six months.

Can Chief Minister be member of Legislative Council where it exists? → Yes.

Who administers CM's oath? → Governor.

Does Chief Minister have a fixed constitutional tenure? → No.

On what does CM's continuation depend? → Confidence of Legislative Assembly.

What happens when Chief Minister resigns? → Entire Council of Ministers ordinarily ceases.

Who chooses State Ministers in practice? → Chief Minister.

Who formally appoints them? → Governor.

Who allocates portfolios? → Chief Minister, formally given effect through constitutional Government procedure.

Which Article contains CM's duties towards Governor? → Article 167.

What must CM communicate under Article 167? → Council decisions, administrative matters and legislative proposals.

Must CM provide information requested by Governor? → Yes.

Can Governor require an individual Minister's decision to be placed before Council? → Yes, through Chief Minister under Article 167.

Which Article deals with conduct of State Government business? → Article 166.

In whose name are State executive actions expressed? → Governor's name.

What is maximum size of State Council of Ministers under the attachment? → 15% of Assembly strength.

Which Amendment imposed this limit? → 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003.

What minimum number of State Ministers is stated in the reference? → 12.

Does Constitution expressly classify Cabinet Ministers, Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers? → No.

What is Cabinet? → Smaller senior decision-making core within Council of Ministers.

Which Article provides for Advocate General? → Article 165.

Who appoints Advocate General? → Governor.

Who is State's highest law officer? → Advocate General.

What qualification must Advocate General possess? → Qualification for appointment as High Court Judge.

Does Advocate General have fixed tenure? → No.

During whose pleasure does Advocate General hold office? → Governor.

Can Advocate General speak in State Legislature? → Yes.

Can Advocate General vote merely because of office? → No.

Which Article allows Governor to summon and prorogue State Legislature and dissolve Assembly? → Article 174.

Which Article gives Governor right to address and send messages? → Article 175.

Which Article provides Special Address? → Article 176.

When does Governor specially address Legislature? → First session after every General Election and first session each year.

Which Article governs Governor's assent to State Bills? → Article 200.

What options are identified in the attachment under Article 200? → Assent, withhold assent, return an eligible non-Money Bill, or reserve Bill for President.

Which Article governs a Bill reserved for President? → Article 201.

Which Article gives Governor Ordinance power? → Article 213.

How long does an Ordinance continue after Legislature reassembles without approval? → Six weeks.

Is Ordinance power normally independent Governor discretion? → No; normally exercised on ministerial advice.

Whose recommendation is required before introducing a State Money Bill? → Governor.

Who appoints State Election Commissioner? → Governor under Article 243K.

Who appoints State PSC Chairperson and members? → Governor under Article 316.

What should be done if Government majority is doubtful? → Floor Test.

Can Governor decide majority merely through personal assessment? → No.

Which case is the leading authority on floor test and Article 356 review? → S.R. Bommai v. Union of India, 1994.

Which case established that Governor ordinarily acts on ministerial advice? → Shamsher Singh v. State of Punjab, 1974.

Which case permitted appointment of a non-legislator as CM subject to six-month rule? → Har Sharan Verma v. Tribhuvan Narain Singh, 1971.

Which case dealt with premature dissolution of Bihar Assembly? → Rameshwar Prasad v. Union of India, 2006.

Which case held removal of Governor cannot be arbitrary or capricious? → B.P. Singhal v. Union of India, 2010.

Which case restricted Governor's interference in legislative proceedings? → Nabam Rebia v. Deputy Speaker, 2016.

Which 2020 case reaffirmed Floor Test as method to determine majority? → Shivraj Singh Chouhan v. Speaker.

Which case stated defection petitions should ordinarily be decided within three months? → Keisham Meghachandra Singh, 2020.

What did Sarkaria Commission recommend regarding Governors? → Neutrality, Floor Test and restrained use of Article 356.

What did Punchhi Commission emphasise? → Clearer discretionary guidelines, transparency, tenure protection and cooperative federalism.

What is the easiest Governor–CM distinction? → Governor is the Constitutional Head; Chief Minister is the Real Executive.
